title: AI Capex & Hyperscaler Investment Outlook I J.P. Morgan
text:
AI Capex & Hyperscaler Investment Outlook I J.P. Morgan

# What unprecedented AI capex means for markets and investors

October 19, 2026

 AI capital expenditures are projected to approach $1 trillion in 2026. How much bigger could it get — and how much longer will this growth go on? 

## Key takeaways

- J.P. Morgan Global Research projects global spending on AI capex to reach $5.5 trillion by 2030 and for $900 billion to be spent in 2026 alone.
- Revenue from cloud service providers has become the most salient data supporting the investment thesis for AI capex, with revenue run-rates showing year-over-year gains and future contracted revenues projecting solid growth.
- The shift in financing from free cash flow to debt, including bond and equity raises, offers a clear window into investor appetite to fund AI capex.
- Bottlenecks ranging from memory and GPU supply to permitting and public opinion represent real challenges to the pace and profitability of AI capex.

The five American hyperscalers — Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and Microsoft — are currently on track to spend roughly as much on AI capex in 2026 alone as they have spent cumulatively since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. After another strong earnings season for hyperscalers in mid-year, that number was revised upward, from $736 billion to $900 billion. “The surge in AI capex-related expenditures has been the defining feature of our economic times,” according to J.P. Morgan chief U.S. economist Michael Feroli.

By 2030, J.P. Morgan Global Research expects the total amount of spending on AI capex to have reached $5 trillion. What forces are working for and against these lofty projections? 

“The surge in AI capex-related expenditures has been the defining feature of our economic times.” 

Michael Feroli 

Chief U.S. economist, J.P. Morgan

## AI capex: A global growth story still in the making

Some American-headquartered hyperscaler companies have tended to dominate the conversation around AI capex. Recently, however, the narrative has gone global, with increased activity from both global and local companies in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), Asia Pacific (APAC) and Latin America (LATAM). Completed and soon-to-be-completed projects across these geographies illustrate this expansion:

- South Africa: Teraco, a data center provider based in South Africa, completed an expansion in Johannesburg that added 30 MW of capacity specifically designed to support high-density AI and cloud workloads.
- Qatar: Meeza, a Qatari data center provider, completed a 4 MW data center expansion project on behalf of an anonymous global hyperscaler, and inked another deal to build 8 MW as of September 2026.
- Malaysia: Vantage Data Centers, a U.S.-based company, operates three primary campuses outside Kuala Lumpur.
- Thailand: Alibaba Cloud opened its second data center in Thailand in 2025, marking a significant expansion of Chinese hyperscaler infrastructure in Southeast Asia.
- Brazil: ByteDance, the owner of TikTok, is spending about $39 billion on one data center on Brazil’s northeast coast, according to a report from Inc. If completed, it will be the largest data center operated by ByteDance outside China.
- Mexico: “Mexico is emerging as a hardware and manufacturing hub within the AI ecosystem,” said Adrian Huerta, head of Mexico Equity Strategy at J.P. Morgan. Huerta noted that tech-related shipments from Mexico have risen from 36% of total country exports in 2023 to 48% today, generating an estimated $10.9 billion trade surplus as of September 2026.

In additional to buildout, global policy is starting to align behind the AI capex wave. In June 2026, the European Commission unveiled the European Technological Sovereignty Package (ETSP), a measure designed to reduce reliance on non-EU suppliers for digital technologies and accelerate AI infrastructure investment. The Cloud and AI Development Act, which was part of the ETSP, specifically aims to triple EU data center capacity within 5–7 years.

The EU has also launched tenders to build up to seven AI gigafactories — massive, purpose-built computing buildings that can house over 100,000 specialized AI chips, draw more than a gigawatt of power and are designed for training and deploying frontier artificial intelligence models. Seven sites have been targeted and over €10 billion in public funding mobilized, with construction expected to start in 2027.

## Cloud storage revenue is driving early returns on AI capex

With so much invested, the market has been eager to see quantifiable returns on AI capex outlays. So far, those returns have come via revenue growth for cloud service providers (CSPs), which function as separate divisions within the organizations of several major hyperscalers:

### Amazon (Amazon Web Services, or AWS) 

AWS revenue grew 37% year over year as of August 2026, reaching an annualized run rate of around $169 billion. Backlog, in the form of future contracted revenues, expanded to $496 billion, indicating that revenue growth is likely to remain consistent for years to come.

### Microsoft (Azure) 

Azure revenue accelerated 43% year over year as of August 2026, increasing from roughly $10 billion in the first quarter of 2023 to around $31 billion in the fourth quarter of 2026 to surpass $100 billion annually. Backlog numbers indicate that growth is expected to continue in the mid-40% range.

### Alphabet (Google Cloud) 

Google Cloud revenue grew 82% year over year as of August 2026, with backlog reaching $514 billion. Operating income for Google Cloud tripled, and GenAI product revenue was up ~800% year-over-year, with a doubling in the number of deals between $100 million and $1 billion. 

### Oracle (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI) 

OCI revenue increased from $2.1 billion in the first quarter of 2025 to $5.8 billion in the fourth quarter of 2026, a 2.7x rise in less than two years. The pace of OCI’s revenue expansion reached 93% year over year, outpacing other hyperscalers.

### Alibaba (Alibaba Cloud) 

Chinese hyperscaler Alibaba reported external cloud revenue growth of 45% year over year as of June 2026 in Alibaba Cloud, the ninth consecutive quarter of acceleration, and said it expects external cloud growth to exceed 50% in the ensuing quarters. Management also highlighted the unit economics of the capex investment paying for itself in under three years.

“The bottom line is that while it may still be too early to declare victory on AI capex ROI, the green shoots are clearly evident,” said Harlan Sur, an equity analyst covering semiconductors for J.P. Morgan. “We expect these trends to remain intact, with improving returns providing a strong economic incentive for hyperscalers and cloud providers to sustain and grow spending.”

## AI capex-related pressure on free cash flow has increased reliance on debt and equity financing

In the early parts of the AI capex buildout, financing came primarily from the free cash flow generated by hyperscalers. Recently, that narrative has started to shift, with high-profile debt and equity raises coming from Google, Oracle and other major hyperscalers in 2025 and 2026, primarily to fund data center buildout.

Dubravko Lakos-Bujas, head of Global Markets Strategy at J.P. Morgan, believes investor appetite to fund AI capex is far from exhausted. “The high-grade market still has substantial capacity to absorb future issuance, although spreads may continue to adjust as supply expectations evolve,” said Lakos-Bujas. “Funding sources are also beginning to broaden towards equity, with Alphabet raising $85 billion in equity in June 2026 and recent (media) reports indicating that Meta is evaluating similar alternatives.”

Importantly, the increase in external financing is not believed to be weakening the operating fundamentals of hyperscalers, for which operating cash flow is still expected to exceed $900 billion by 2027. “In effect, the Street appears to be underwriting the AI data center monetization case: elevated capex today should ultimately translate into higher revenue, stronger margins and expanding cash flow,” said Lakos-Bujas.

“In effect, the Street appears to be underwriting the AI data center monetization case: elevated capex today should ultimately translate into higher revenue, stronger margins and expanding cash flow.”

Dubravko Lakos-Bujas 

Head of Global Markets Strategy, J.P. Morgan

## Other factors beyond financing limit the pace of the AI capex buildout

Beyond questions around financing, several factors have emerged as meaningful roadblocks for AI capex:

Power availability and infrastructure

- Securing sufficient, reliable power remains the primary bottleneck for AI capex, due largely to the amount and density of energy required to power data centers, as well as their need for land and proximity to water. Upgrades to grid infrastructure and access to renewable energy are often slow and costly, impacting project timelines and scalability.
- “The surge in AI workloads is driving a step change in power demand, with data centers projected to account for 9%–17% of total U.S. electricity demand by 2030, up from 3%–4% today,” said Tarek Hamid, head of the North American Corporate Credit Research team at J.P. Morgan. “Globally, data center electricity consumption is expected to more than double by 2030, with the U.S. and China leading incremental demand.”

Equipment supply and accelerated depreciation

- Long lead times for critical equipment — including graphics processing units, or GPUs, along with memory modules, cooling systems and power solutions — represent another major constraint. Currently, a memory shortage is driving up the cost of DRAM, or dynamic random access memory, which is used in AI inferencing and model training. Amazon’s $20 billion increase in its capex guidance for 2026 was attributed largely to increased memory costs.
- “AI infrastructure relies on rapidly advancing chips and systems,” said Feroli. “As newer generations deliver better performance and lower cost per unit of compute, older hardware loses economic value faster than conventional equipment.” In other words, AI capex can advance so rapidly that chips, hardware and even models become obsolete faster than traditional hardware and machinery, making the true value of these goods more difficult to ascertain.

Construction and labor

- Data center construction cycles typically run 18–30 months, and can be further delayed by shortages of skilled labor, permitting challenges and rising construction costs, slowing the delivery of new capacity and triggering inventory adjustments across the supply chain.

Regulatory developments

- Permitting, environmental regulations and land availability often delay projects, especially in high-demand regions. Increasingly, public backlash and municipal or state moratoriums are also forcing developers to seek alternative sites as public and political debate continues. Much of this opposition is rooted in consumer concerns: as data centers draw on local grids, residents and policymakers are increasingly focused on the effect on household electricity bills and grid reliability. In several markets, that has shifted the debate toward who bears the cost of new capacity — with proposals to place more of the incremental infrastructure expense on developers rather than ratepayers.
- “Data center expansion is no longer just an engineering-scarcity story; it’s a political economy question of who gets power, who funds upgrades, and who accepts the local impacts,” said Hannah Lee, an equity analyst covering APAC Thematic and Sustainable Investing Research at J.P. Morgan. “As those constraints stack, approval timelines and delivered costs become harder to predict and more dispersed.”
